gist: Wildfires in northern boreal regions are accelerating permafrost thaw and releasing ancient carbon.
Scientists and agencies are studying fire suppression and cultural burning to protect frozen soil.
New satellite networks and mapping are being developed to detect and target high-risk blazes.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Intensifying wildfires across northern boreal forests have accelerated permafrost thaw, leading researchers and fire managers to test intervention strategies. In regions like Alaska, initiatives are trialling fire suppression and intentional burning to safeguard carbon-dense soils rather than solely defending human habitations and property.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Permafrost stores roughly twice as much carbon as the atmosphere. Intense blazes burn away the insulating organic topsoil, causing rapid thaw and releasing potent greenhouse gases. This threatens to create a feedback loop that transforms northern carbon sinks into major global emission sources.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Collaborators under the North Fire initiative plan to expand risk mapping across Alaska and Canada and test cultural burning near Fort Yukon. Meanwhile, the FireSat satellite constellation will expand into the 2030s to help detect blazes early.
